title: Strategic synthesis of FLPClusters toward catalysis

paper_content.abstract:
FLPClusters, which are structurally precise metal clusters incorporating Frustrated
Lewis Pairs (FLPs), represent a promising class of FLP catalysts. Although FLPClusters have
emerged only recently, their precise and strategic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Herein, we
report the approach for the strategic synthesis of FLPClusters featuring well-defined, tailorable,
and accessible FLP active sites. Our approach utilizes bis(2-(diphenylphosphino)phenyl)ether
(DPEphos) as a rigid surface ligand. The two phosphine termini of DPEphos bridge adjacent metal
atoms, while the central ether oxygen atom (Lewis base) is geometrically constrained, enabling
the formation of stable FLPs with copper atoms (Lewis acid) on the cluster surface. By modulating
the structure of ancillary thiolate ligands, we successfully synthesized three FLPClusters.
These
FLPClusters demonstrate high catalytic activity in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to
silanols. Both theoretical and experimental studies confirm that the catalysis is FLP-driven.
Crucially, their catalytic performance scales with the number of FLP sites present.
paper_content.introduction:
Frustrated Lewis Pairs (FLPs) have attracted significant interest in chemical and materials
science.1-3 Comprising sterically or geometrically hindered Lewis acid (LA) and Lewis base (LB)
sites that cannot undergo classical adduct formation, FLPs exhibit a distinctive “push-pull” effect.4-
6 This enables efficient activation of diverse small molecules—including H , CO , SO , N O, NO,
2 2 2 2
and CO—leading to catalytic capabilities.7-10 A key advantage of FLPs lies in their exceptional
design flexibility: LB donors (e.g., N, O, S) and LA acceptors (e.g., B, Al, Ce, other metal centers)
offer broad tunability.11-14 Furthermore, the FLP concept extends beyond homogeneous catalysis,
proving compatible with heterogeneous systems such as zeolites, metal oxide surfaces, and
metal/covalent organic frameworks.15-17 These heterogeneous FLP catalysts demonstrate
remarkable efficiency and recyclability in small-molecule activation.18-21

The FLP concept has recently been introduced into the field of ligand-protected, atomically
precise noble metal clusters (designated as FLPClusters).22 Representing a promising class of
inorganic-organic hybrid materials, ligand-protected noble metal clusters exhibit broad
applications.23-32 Their atomically precise molecular structures, exceptional catalytic performance
across diverse chemical transformations, and structure-dependent catalytic properties establish
them as ideal model systems for investigating structure-catalysis relationships and reaction
mechanisms.33-37 Surface functionalization with tailored ligands has emerged as a strategy to create
FLP sites and enhance the catalytic performance of these metal clusters. For example,
incorporating 2-methoxybenzenethiolate ligands onto the [Cu S (RS) (PPh ) ]2+ cluster (Cu ,
34 7 18 3 4 34
RSH = 2-methoxybenzenethiol) facilitates the formation of FLPs between surface copper atoms
(acting as LAs) and the oxygen atoms of the ligands (acting as LBs).22 These precisely positioned
FLPs, stabilized by the well-defined surface coordination environment, enable efficient heterolytic
H activation. This capability leads to notable catalytic efficiency in regioselective hydrogenation
2
reactions.

Despite preliminary advances, a fundamental limitation persists in the previous Cu
34
FLPCluster system. Unlike previously reported FLP catalysts where LAs and LBs are
systematically organized via steric or electronic control, Cu exhibits significantly diminished
34
FLP formation.38,39 As illustrated in Figure 1 (previous work), most 2-methoxybenzenethiolate
ligands preferentially form thermodynamically stable O–Cu adducts instead of participating in
FLP assembly. This behavior arises from the ligands’ inherent conformational flexibility and
insufficient steric constraints, highlighting the persistent challenges in FLPCluster design. To
overcome this limitation, we focused on bis(2-diphenylphosphinophenyl)ether (DPEphos). As
widely documented, DPEphos possesses distinctive structural properties as a bidentate ligand, with
its central oxygen atom adopting an uncoordinated, pendant configuration.40,41 When assembled
on metal cluster surfaces, DPEphos exhibits optimal coordination behavior: its two phosphine
termini selectively bridge adjacent surface metal atoms, while the strategically positioned central
oxygen atom (LB) remains spatially constrained, thereby forming stable FLPs with surface metal
atoms (LAs).42 The intrinsic rigidity of the DPEphos framework ensures full participation of all
oxygen centers in FLP formation, enabling the construction of well-defined FLPClusters with
precise architectural control (Figure 1, this work). Guided by this design principle, the synthesized
triple-cluster system demonstrates that FLPClusters not only exhibit outstanding catalytic
efficiency in organic transformations but also display a near-linear correlation between catalytic
activity and the number of FLP active sites.

identity of the thiolate ligand. Specifically, the reaction system utilizing p-nitrothiophenol (R S)

FLPClusters-driven hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to silanols. Building upon the
superior water activation capability demonstrated by Cu , we investigated its catalytic utility in the
4
selective hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to silanols. Silanols containing Si-OH
functionalities are pivotal intermediates in organic synthesis.55 While gold and silver nanoparticles
can catalyze this transformation,56,57 the development of cost-effective, earth-abundant copper-
based nanocatalysts capable of utilizing water as a benign oxidant remains an unaddressed
challenge.55

To evaluate catalytic performance, the Cu cluster was immobilized on Vulcan XC-72 carbon
4
black via a solution impregnation method (details see METHODS SECTION). The catalytic
reaction was conducted in an air-saturated acetone/water mixture, with reaction progress
monitored in real-time by gas chromatography (GC). As envisioned, the resulting Cu /XC-72
4
catalyst (1% loading) demonstrated exceptional efficiency, achieving near-quantitative conversion
of triethylsilane within 24h at 50 oC (Figure 5a). Importantly, the catalyst exhibited excellent
cycling stability, with no appreciable decay in activity observed over six consecutive cycles (18h
each) (Figure 5b).

To confirm the structural stability of the catalysts, a suite of characterization techniques was
employed. The structural evolution of the clusters under operating conditions was probed by X-
ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure
(EXAFS) measurements at the Cu K-edge. The spectral profiles of Cu remained virtually identical
4
before and after loading onto carbon black, confirming that immobilization did not alter the
cluster’s nuclearity or geometry (Figure S37a). Crucially, the XANES and EXAFS features of the
catalyst were preserved after the reaction (Figure S37b, c). Quantitative EXAFS fitting (Figure
S38 and Table S5) revealed no significant deviations in the coordination numbers or bond lengths
of the Cu–Cu, Cu–S and Cu–P shells, proving that the cluster framework remains intact without
aggregation or fragmentation. This conclusion is corroborated by transmission electron
microscopy (TEM), which showed no formation of metal nanoparticles, and XPS and FTIR
spectroscopy, which verified the preservation of the Cu oxidation state and ligand coordination
environment (Figures S39–S42).

Comparative analysis identifies the engineered surface FLP sites as the sole origin of the
enhanced catalytic activity. The DPEphos ligand plays a dual role: it passivates the cluster to
maintain structural integrity while its central oxygen atom acts as a geometrically constrained
Lewis base, cooperating with surface copper atoms to form active FLP sites. To rigorously verify
this mechanism, we designed a series of control experiments (Figure 5c). Neither the carbon black
support nor the free DPEphos ligand exhibited significant activity (conversions < 5%). Similarly,
physical mixtures of copper salts and DPEphos showed negligible activity (5.8%). These results
collectively rule out the carbon support, free ligands, or unstructured copper species as active
contributors. Compelling evidence is provided by structurally well-defined Cu derivatives

(6.4%), and Cu (7.3%)) showed negligible activity (Figures 5c, S44 and S45).60-64 These findings

cluster core, but originates exclusively from the geometrically well-defined FLP sites established
by the precise coordination of DPEphos to the surface copper centers. Notably, the Cu /XC-72
4

diverse silane substrates with equally high efficiency (Figure 5d). Impressively, the catalyst
achieves complete oxidation of both sterically hindered alkylsilanes and electronically distinct
arylsilanes without observable differences in rate attributable to steric effects.

Reaction mechanism of silane hydrolysis catalyzed by FLPClusters. To fully elucidate
the fundamental characteristics of surface FLPs and their catalytic mechanism, we adopted an
integrated approach combining experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT)
calculations. Initially, molecular probe-based active site blocking experiments were conducted to
investigate the active site dependence of the catalytic reaction. Previous studies have demonstrated
that exogenous LAs or LBs can competitively bind to surface FLP sites, thereby significantly
inhibiting their catalytic activity.65 As demonstrated in Figure 6a, the competitive introduction of
either LA inhibitors (pyrrole, boric acid) or LB inhibitors (pyridine, thiourea) into the reaction
system resulted in marked decreases in catalytic activity. These findings confirm the indispensable
role of bifunctional Cu⋯O FLP sites in the oxidative transformation of organosilanes, establishing
the crucial promoting effect of synergistic Lewis acid-base interactions on reaction conversion.

Our investigations conclusively identified the FLPs within the Cu cluster as the primary
4
active sites responsible for the observed catalytic transformation. This finding strongly suggests a
direct correlation between the catalytic activity of the FLPCluster system and the number of
accessible FLP sites. To rigorously verify this hypothesis, we loaded Cu and Cu clusters-each
22 28
confirmed by structural analysis to possess three well-defined FLP sites—onto carbon black
supports with an equivalent molar amount of FLP sites. Under identical reaction conditions,
catalytic test over a 6-hour period revealed significantly enhanced activity for both clusters,
reaching 1.5 and 1.5 times the benchmark activity of Cu , respectively (Figure 6b). Notably,
4
despite the differences in their overall size and structure, Cu and Cu clusters, which harbor the
22 28
identical number (three) of FLP sites, demonstrated remarkably comparable molar catalytic
activities. This key observation provides compelling evidence that the catalytic efficiency is
predominantly governed by the quantity of accessible FLP rather than the total cluster size or
structure. This conclusion is further reinforced by concentration-dependent experiments using the
Cu
4
catalyst: as the catalyst mass increased incrementally from 20 mg to 80 mg (maintaining a
constant loading ratio), the 6-hour conversion rates progressively rose from 15.6% to 32.6% and
68.4%, unambiguously demonstrating the dominant role of active site quantity in driving reaction
conversion (Figure S46). These collective results establish a critical and quantifiable relationship:
the catalytic efficiency on the surfaces of these copper clusters is intimately linked to, and primarily
determined by, the abundance of available FLP sites. This fundamental understanding provides a
robust foundation for the rational design and synthesis of next-generation, high-performance
copper cluster catalysts by strategically maximizing the density of these catalytically active FLP
centers.

To complement the experimental findings, we performed DFT calculations incorporating
Grimme’s dispersion correction to elucidate the reaction mechanism and determine accurate

indicate they are catalytically inactive; water dissociation on these sites faces a prohibitively high
activation barrier of 2.36 eV (Figure S47), significantly higher than that of the Cu···O pathway.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Zheng and coworkers reported the synthesis and characterization of three distinct copper-based sila (FLP) clusters. This is a highly robust and compelling study. The well-defined structures demonstrate exceptional catalytic performance and outstanding stability in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes. This work is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after major revisions.
1. The authors employed Cu(II) nitrate as the sole copper precursor in the synthesis of FLP clusters for catalysis. How about the reactivity of other copper sources? Was there any particular consideration for not using Cu(I) species? How about the use of Cu(I) affect the formation and catalytic performance of the resulting clusters? If possible, please provide more information for the synthesis of FLPClusters.
2.The synthesis of FLP clusters in this work appears to rely exclusively on DPPOE as the best ligand. What was the basis for not screening other bisphosphine ligands? Were other ligands incompatible with the cluster formation process? If possible, please provide more information for the difference of other phosphine ligands.
3.The application of the synthesized catalysts in the hydrolytic oxidation of silanes is interesting. However, it was found that chlorosilanes (e.g., 2c, 2f) can also be applied in this reaction. It is difficult to understand the experiment results because chlorosilanes are highly sensitive to hydrolysis in air and might be occurred with polymerization, it is a serious question that how to determine the formation of such products?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript reports the synthesis of FLPClusters—structurally defined metal clusters incorporating frustrated Lewis pairs (FLPs), and their application in catalysis. While the study presents interesting results and the topic is timely, the novelty appears limited, as the work seems to be a direct continuation of the group’s earlier publication from last year. More importantly, there are several inconsistencies and missing controls, particularly in the catalytic evaluation and stability studies, that prevent the work from meeting the standards for publication in Nature Communications.
1)The clusters are deposited on carbon black, yet no blank catalytic tests are presented with carbon black alone or with carbon black + ligand. Such controls are essential to rule out contributions from the support or ligand alone.
2)The manuscript claims recyclability and stability, but there is no convincing evidence that the cluster structure and ligand shell remain intact after deposition and catalytic runs. No characterization of the supported clusters is shown. The interaction between the cluster and ligands, which is central to the proposed mechanism, is not experimentally validated.
3)The comparison with non-functionalized clusters is vague. The manuscript simply mentions them without details or quantitative data, which weakens the claim of superior performance.
4)The catalytic activity is reported to persist or even improve over 6 hours, but no mechanistic explanation is provided. This raises the possibility of cluster modification, leaching, or restructuring under reaction conditions, which should be addressed with appropriate post-reaction characterization. Additional details are needed to confirm the structural integrity of the clusters after deposition and catalysis.
5) Atomically precise clusters are known to display size-dependent catalytic properties, sometimes even with single-atom differences. Surprisingly, the authors report no differences across clusters of different sizes. This contradiction requires explanation. If the activity is solely attributed to the ligands, then one must also consider testing the ligands alone on the support.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript presents a well-designed study on the development of three distinct copper FLPClusters: Cu4(DPPOE)2(R1S)4, [Cu22H7(DPPOE)3(R1S)16]- and Cu28H9(DPPOE)3(R2S)18. These clusters exhibit good catalytic activity and stability in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes. A detailed molecular structural analysis reveals that the bulky nature of the DPPOE ligand sterically encumbers the central oxygen atom, acting as a Lewis base, while Cu(I) serves as a Lewis acid. This work is innovative, methodologically sound, and addresses a significant gap in the field of FLPClusters. The results are scientifically significant, with promising yields and recyclability.
During revision, the authors might consider the following comments:
1. Only Cu4 clusters have been characterised for Lewis acidity and basicity using theoretical and experimental methods, such as DRIFT. Similar analyses should be conducted on other clusters, like Cu28 and Cu22, to identify the optimal LA-LB pair.
2. The authors link catalytic activity to the number of FLP sites, but only two types were studied, which is insufficient to support this claim. Additional experiments, such as varying catalyst concentration, are recommended to clarify this point.
3. The authors noted that changing DPPOE amounts produced different types of FLPClusters, with a possibility of mixed clusters. What is their perspective on this?
4. On page 17, the authors note that Cu22 and Cu28 both have three FLP active sites, yet Cu28 shows higher catalytic activity. Is there another factor besides FLP active sites?
5. It appears that the stability of the FLP clusters increases with greater ligand bulkiness. Have the authors considered utilising alternative bulky ligands or derivatives of DPPOE in similar experiments?
6. For the catalytic comparison study, the author should consider selecting copper clusters with similar atomic numbers rather than using random clusters. Using Cu4 with different ligands may be more appropriate for comparison in this study.
7. Ligand-protected nanoclusters typically exhibit a core-shell structure, with the metal in the core as M(0) and in the shell as M(I). However, the authors state that all copper sites in Cu28 (Figures S20-S21) are in the +1 oxidation state. This raises the question: what drives the stability of these nanoclusters, particularly during catalysis?
8. Since hydrogen, a reductant, is produced as a side product during catalysis, the copper site may be reduced. To confirm its oxidation state, the author should perform XPS or Auger analysis.

## Abstract

FLPClusters, which are structurally precise metal clusters incorporating Frustrated
Lewis Pairs (FLPs), represent a promising class of FLP catalysts. Although FLPClusters have
emerged only recently, their precise and strategic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Herein, we
report the approach for the strategic synthesis of FLPClusters featuring well-defined, tailorable,
and accessible FLP active sites. Our approach utilizes bis(2-(diphenylphosphino)phenyl)ether
(DPEphos) as a rigid surface ligand. The two phosphine termini of DPEphos bridge adjacent metal
atoms, while the central ether oxygen atom (Lewis base) is geometrically constrained, enabling
the formation of stable FLPs with copper atoms (Lewis acid) on the cluster surface. By modulating
the structure of ancillary thiolate ligands, we successfully synthesized three FLPClusters.
These
FLPClusters demonstrate high catalytic activity in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to
silanols. Both theoretical and experimental studies confirm that the catalysis is FLP-driven.
Crucially, their catalytic performance scales with the number of FLP sites present.

---

## Introduction

Frustrated Lewis Pairs (FLPs) have attracted significant interest in chemical and materials
science.1-3 Comprising sterically or geometrically hindered Lewis acid (LA) and Lewis base (LB)
sites that cannot undergo classical adduct formation, FLPs exhibit a distinctive “push-pull” effect.4-
6 This enables efficient activation of diverse small molecules—including H , CO , SO , N O, NO,
2 2 2 2
and CO—leading to catalytic capabilities.7-10 A key advantage of FLPs lies in their exceptional
design flexibility: LB donors (e.g., N, O, S) and LA acceptors (e.g., B, Al, Ce, other metal centers)
offer broad tunability.11-14 Furthermore, the FLP concept extends beyond homogeneous catalysis,
proving compatible with heterogeneous systems such as zeolites, metal oxide surfaces, and
metal/covalent organic frameworks.15-17 These heterogeneous FLP catalysts demonstrate
remarkable efficiency and recyclability in small-molecule activation.18-21

The FLP concept has recently been introduced into the field of ligand-protected, atomically
precise noble metal clusters (designated as FLPClusters).22 Representing a promising class of
inorganic-organic hybrid materials, ligand-protected noble metal clusters exhibit broad
applications.23-32 Their atomically precise molecular structures, exceptional catalytic performance
across diverse chemical transformations, and structure-dependent catalytic properties establish
them as ideal model systems for investigating structure-catalysis relationships and reaction
mechanisms.33-37 Surface functionalization with tailored ligands has emerged as a strategy to create
FLP sites and enhance the catalytic performance of these metal clusters. For example,
incorporating 2-methoxybenzenethiolate ligands onto the [Cu S (RS) (PPh ) ]2+ cluster (Cu ,

To evaluate catalytic performance, the Cu cluster was immobilized on Vulcan XC-72 carbon
4

reaction was conducted in an air-saturated acetone/water mixture, with reaction progress
monitored in real-time by gas chromatography (GC). As envisioned, the resulting Cu /XC-72
4
catalyst (1% loading) demonstrated exceptional efficiency, achieving near-quantitative conversion
of triethylsilane within 24h at 50 oC (Figure 5a). Importantly, the catalyst exhibited excellent

To confirm the structural stability of the catalysts, a suite of characterization techniques was
employed. The structural evolution of the clusters under operating conditions was probed by X-

4

environment (Figures S39–S42).

support nor the free DPEphos ligand exhibited significant activity (conversions < 5%). Similarly,

Reaction mechanism of silane hydrolysis catalyzed by FLPClusters. To fully elucidate
the fundamental characteristics of surface FLPs and their catalytic mechanism, we adopted an
integrated approach combining experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT)
calculations. Initially, molecular probe-based active site blocking experiments were conducted to
investigate the active site dependence of the catalytic reaction. Previous studies have demonstrated
that exogenous LAs or LBs can competitively bind to surface FLP sites, thereby significantly
inhibiting their catalytic activity.65 As demonstrated in Figure 6a, the competitive introduction of
either LA inhibitors (pyrrole, boric acid) or LB inhibitors (pyridine, thiourea) into the reaction
system resulted in marked decreases in catalytic activity. These findings confirm the indispensable
role of bifunctional Cu⋯O FLP sites in the oxidative transformation of organosilanes, establishing
the crucial promoting effect of synergistic Lewis acid-base interactions on reaction conversion.

Our investigations conclusively identified the FLPs within the Cu cluster as the primary
4
active sites responsible for the observed catalytic transformation. This finding strongly suggests a
direct correlation between the catalytic activity of the FLPCluster system and the number of
accessible FLP sites. To rigorously verify this hypothesis, we loaded Cu and Cu clusters-each
22 28
confirmed by structural analysis to possess three well-defined FLP sites—onto carbon black
supports with an equivalent molar amount of FLP sites. Under identical reaction conditions,
catalytic test over a 6-hour period revealed significantly enhanced activity for both clusters,
reaching 1.5 and 1.5 times the benchmark activity of Cu , respectively (Figure 6b). Notably,
4
despite the differences in their overall size and structure, Cu and Cu clusters, which harbor the
22 28
identical number (three) of FLP sites, demonstrated remarkably comparable molar catalytic
activities. This key observation provides compelling evidence that the catalytic efficiency is
predominantly governed by the quantity of accessible FLP rather than the total cluster size or
structure. This conclusion is further reinforced by concentration-dependent experiments using the
Cu
4
catalyst: as the catalyst mass increased incrementally from 20 mg to 80 mg (maintaining a
constant loading ratio), the 6-hour conversion rates progressively rose from 15.6% to 32.6% and
68.4%, unambiguously demonstrating the dominant role of active site quantity in driving reaction
conversion (Figure S46). These collective results establish a critical and quantifiable relationship:
the catalytic efficiency on the surfaces of these copper clusters is intimately linked to, and primarily
determined by, the abundance of available FLP sites. This fundamental understanding provides a
robust foundation for the rational design and synthesis of next-generation, high-performance
copper cluster catalysts by strategically maximizing the density of these catalytically active FLP
centers.

To complement the experimental findings, we performed DFT calculations incorporating
Grimme’s dispersion correction to elucidate the reaction mechanism and determine accurate

heterolytic cleavage: the hydroxyl group (OH) adsorbs on the copper center (LA site), while the

indicate they are catalytically inactive; water dissociation on these sites faces a prohibitively high
activation barrier of 2.36 eV (Figure S47), significantly higher than that of the Cu···O pathway.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Zheng and coworkers reported the synthesis and characterization of three distinct copper-based sila (FLP) clusters. This is a highly robust and compelling study. The well-defined structures demonstrate exceptional catalytic performance and outstanding stability in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes. This work is suitable for publication in Nature Communications after major revisions.
1. The authors employed Cu(II) nitrate as the sole copper precursor in the synthesis of FLP clusters for catalysis. How about the reactivity of other copper sources? Was there any particular consideration for not using Cu(I) species? How about the use of Cu(I) affect the formation and catalytic performance of the resulting clusters? If possible, please provide more information for the synthesis of FLPClusters.
2.The synthesis of FLP clusters in this work appears to rely exclusively on DPPOE as the best ligand. What was the basis for not screening other bisphosphine ligands? Were other ligands incompatible with the cluster formation process? If possible, please provide more information for the difference of other phosphine ligands.
3.The application of the synthesized catalysts in the hydrolytic oxidation of silanes is interesting. However, it was found that chlorosilanes (e.g., 2c, 2f) can also be applied in this reaction. It is difficult to understand the experiment results because chlorosilanes are highly sensitive to hydrolysis in air and might be occurred with polymerization, it is a serious question that how to determine the formation of such products?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports the synthesis of FLPClusters—structurally defined metal clusters incorporating frustrated Lewis pairs (FLPs), and their application in catalysis. While the study presents interesting results and the topic is timely, the novelty appears limited, as the work seems to be a direct continuation of the group’s earlier publication from last year. More importantly, there are several inconsistencies and missing controls, particularly in the catalytic evaluation and stability studies, that prevent the work from meeting the standards for publication in Nature Communications.
1)The clusters are deposited on carbon black, yet no blank catalytic tests are presented with carbon black alone or with carbon black + ligand. Such controls are essential to rule out contributions from the support or ligand alone.
2)The manuscript claims recyclability and stability, but there is no convincing evidence that the cluster structure and ligand shell remain intact after deposition and catalytic runs. No characterization of the supported clusters is shown. The interaction between the cluster and ligands, which is central to the proposed mechanism, is not experimentally validated.
3)The comparison with non-functionalized clusters is vague. The manuscript simply mentions them without details or quantitative data, which weakens the claim of superior performance.
4)The catalytic activity is reported to persist or even improve over 6 hours, but no mechanistic explanation is provided. This raises the possibility of cluster modification, leaching, or restructuring under reaction conditions, which should be addressed with appropriate post-reaction characterization. Additional details are needed to confirm the structural integrity of the clusters after deposition and catalysis.
5) Atomically precise clusters are known to display size-dependent catalytic properties, sometimes even with single-atom differences. Surprisingly, the authors report no differences across clusters of different sizes. This contradiction requires explanation. If the activity is solely attributed to the ligands, then one must also consider testing the ligands alone on the support.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a well-designed study on the development of three distinct copper FLPClusters: Cu4(DPPOE)2(R1S)4, [Cu22H7(DPPOE)3(R1S)16]- and Cu28H9(DPPOE)3(R2S)18. These clusters exhibit good catalytic activity and stability in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes. A detailed molecular structural analysis reveals that the bulky nature of the DPPOE ligand sterically encumbers the central oxygen atom, acting as a Lewis base, while Cu(I) serves as a Lewis acid. This work is innovative, methodologically sound, and addresses a significant gap in the field of FLPClusters. The results are scientifically significant, with promising yields and recyclability.
During revision, the authors might consider the following comments:
1. Only Cu4 clusters have been characterised for Lewis acidity and basicity using theoretical and experimental methods, such as DRIFT. Similar analyses should be conducted on other clusters, like Cu28 and Cu22, to identify the optimal LA-LB pair.
2. The authors link catalytic activity to the number of FLP sites, but only two types were studied, which is insufficient to support this claim. Additional experiments, such as varying catalyst concentration, are recommended to clarify this point.
3. The authors noted that changing DPPOE amounts produced different types of FLPClusters, with a possibility of mixed clusters. What is their perspective on this?
4. On page 17, the authors note that Cu22 and Cu28 both have three FLP active sites, yet Cu28 shows higher catalytic activity. Is there another factor besides FLP active sites?
5. It appears that the stability of the FLP clusters increases with greater ligand bulkiness. Have the authors considered utilising alternative bulky ligands or derivatives of DPPOE in similar experiments?
6. For the catalytic comparison study, the author should consider selecting copper clusters with similar atomic numbers rather than using random clusters. Using Cu4 with different ligands may be more appropriate for comparison in this study.
7. Ligand-protected nanoclusters typically exhibit a core-shell structure, with the metal in the core as M(0) and in the shell as M(I). However, the authors state that all copper sites in Cu28 (Figures S20-S21) are in the +1 oxidation state. This raises the question: what drives the stability of these nanoclusters, particularly during catalysis?
8. Since hydrogen, a reductant, is produced as a side product during catalysis, the copper site may be reduced. To confirm its oxidation state, the author should perform XPS or Auger analysis.

## Abstract

FLPClusters, which are structurally precise metal clusters incorporating Frustrated
Lewis Pairs (FLPs), represent a promising class of FLP catalysts. Although FLPClusters have
emerged only recently, their precise and strategic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Herein, we
report the approach for the strategic synthesis of FLPClusters featuring well-defined, tailorable,
and accessible FLP active sites. Our approach utilizes bis(2-(diphenylphosphino)phenyl)ether
(DPEphos) as a rigid surface ligand. The two phosphine termini of DPEphos bridge adjacent metal
atoms, while the central ether oxygen atom (Lewis base) is geometrically constrained, enabling
the formation of stable FLPs with copper atoms (Lewis acid) on the cluster surface. By modulating
the structure of ancillary thiolate ligands, we successfully synthesized three FLPClusters.
These
FLPClusters demonstrate high catalytic activity in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to
silanols. Both theoretical and experimental studies confirm that the catalysis is FLP-driven.
Crucially, their catalytic performance scales with the number of FLP sites present.

---

## Introduction

Frustrated Lewis Pairs (FLPs) have attracted significant interest in chemical and materials
science.1-3 Comprising sterically or geometrically hindered Lewis acid (LA) and Lewis base (LB)
sites that cannot undergo classical adduct formation, FLPs exhibit a distinctive “push-pull” effect.4-
6 This enables efficient activation of diverse small molecules—including H , CO , SO , N O, NO,
2 2 2 2
and CO—leading to catalytic capabilities.7-10 A key advantage of FLPs lies in their exceptional
design flexibility: LB donors (e.g., N, O, S) and LA acceptors (e.g., B, Al, Ce, other metal centers)
offer broad tunability.11-14 Furthermore, the FLP concept extends beyond homogeneous catalysis,
proving compatible with heterogeneous systems such as zeolites, metal oxide surfaces, and
metal/covalent organic frameworks.15-17 These heterogeneous FLP catalysts demonstrate
remarkable efficiency and recyclability in small-molecule activation.18-21

The FLP concept has recently been introduced into the field of ligand-protected, atomically
precise noble metal clusters (designated as FLPClusters).22 Representing a promising class of
inorganic-organic hybrid materials, ligand-protected noble metal clusters exhibit broad
applications.23-32 Their atomically precise molecular structures, exceptional catalytic performance
across diverse chemical transformations, and structure-dependent catalytic properties establish
them as ideal model systems for investigating structure-catalysis relationships and reaction
mechanisms.33-37 Surface functionalization with tailored ligands has emerged as a strategy to create
FLP sites and enhance the catalytic performance of these metal clusters. For example,
incorporating 2-methoxybenzenethiolate ligands onto the [Cu S (RS) (PPh ) ]2+ cluster (Cu ,
34 7 18 3 4 34
RSH = 2-methoxybenzenethiol) facilitates the formation of FLPs between surface copper atoms
(acting as LAs) and the oxygen atoms of the ligands (acting as LBs).22 These precisely positioned
FLPs, stabilized by the well-defined surface coordination environment, enable efficient heterolytic
H activation. This capability leads to notable catalytic efficiency in regioselective hydrogenation
2

FLPClusters-driven hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to silanols. Building upon the
superior water activation capability demonstrated by Cu , we investigated its catalytic utility in the
4
selective hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to silanols. Silanols containing Si-OH
functionalities are pivotal intermediates in organic synthesis.55 While gold and silver nanoparticles
can catalyze this transformation,56,57 the development of cost-effective, earth-abundant copper-
based nanocatalysts capable of utilizing water as a benign oxidant remains an unaddressed
challenge.55

To evaluate catalytic performance, the Cu cluster was immobilized on Vulcan XC-72 carbon
4
black via a solution impregnation method (details see METHODS SECTION). The catalytic
reaction was conducted in an air-saturated acetone/water mixture, with reaction progress
monitored in real-time by gas chromatography (GC). As envisioned, the resulting Cu /XC-72
4
catalyst (1% loading) demonstrated exceptional efficiency, achieving near-quantitative conversion
of triethylsilane within 24h at 50 oC (Figure 5a). Importantly, the catalyst exhibited excellent
cycling stability, with no appreciable decay in activity observed over six consecutive cycles (18h
each) (Figure 5b).

To confirm the structural stability of the catalysts, a suite of characterization techniques was
employed. The structural evolution of the clusters under operating conditions was probed by X-
ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure
(EXAFS) measurements at the Cu K-edge. The spectral profiles of Cu remained virtually identical
4
before and after loading onto carbon black, confirming that immobilization did not alter the
cluster’s nuclearity or geometry (Figure S37a). Crucially, the XANES and EXAFS features of the
catalyst were preserved after the reaction (Figure S37b, c). Quantitative EXAFS fitting (Figure
S38 and Table S5) revealed no significant deviations in the coordination numbers or bond lengths
of the Cu–Cu, Cu–S and Cu–P shells, proving that the cluster framework remains intact without
aggregation or fragmentation. This conclusion is corroborated by transmission electron
microscopy (TEM), which showed no formation of metal nanoparticles, and XPS and FTIR
spectroscopy, which verified the preservation of the Cu oxidation state and ligand coordination
environment (Figures S39–S42).

Comparative analysis identifies the engineered surface FLP sites as the sole origin of the
enhanced catalytic activity. The DPEphos ligand plays a dual role: it passivates the cluster to
maintain structural integrity while its central oxygen atom acts as a geometrically constrained
Lewis base, cooperating with surface copper atoms to form active FLP sites. To rigorously verify
this mechanism, we designed a series of control experiments (Figure 5c). Neither the carbon black
support nor the free DPEphos ligand exhibited significant activity (conversions < 5%). Similarly,
physical mixtures of copper salts and DPEphos showed negligible activity (5.8%). These results
collectively rule out the carbon support, free ligands, or unstructured copper species as active
contributors. Compelling evidence is provided by structurally well-defined Cu derivatives
4
stabilized by non-FLP ligands—specifically Cu (PPh Py) Cl and Cu (dpph) (PhC≡C) —which
4 2 4 2 4 2 4
exhibited only moderate activity (7.5% and 8.4% conversion, respectively) due to the absence of
accessible FLP motifs (Figures 5c and S43).58,59 Similarly, conventional copper nanoclusters
passivated by non-functional ligands (Cu (9.5%), Cu (6.2%), Cu (6.8%), Cu (6.0%), Cu
25 26 8 50 12
(6.4%), and Cu (7.3%)) showed negligible activity (Figures 5c, S44 and S45).60-64 These findings
66
collectively demonstrate that the catalytic performance is not an intrinsic property of the copper
cluster core, but originates exclusively from the geometrically well-defined FLP sites established
by the precise coordination of DPEphos to the surface copper centers. Notably, the Cu /XC-72
4
catalyst also exhibits a broad substrate scope under optimized conditions, effectively oxidizing
diverse silane substrates with equally high efficiency (Figure 5d). Impressively, the catalyst
achieves complete oxidation of both sterically hindered alkylsilanes and electronically distinct
arylsilanes without observable differences in rate attributable to steric effects.

Reaction mechanism of silane hydrolysis catalyzed by FLPClusters. To fully elucidate
the fundamental characteristics of surface FLPs and their catalytic mechanism, we adopted an
integrated approach combining experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT)
calculations. Initially, molecular probe-based active site blocking experiments were conducted to
investigate the active site dependence of the catalytic reaction. Previous studies have demonstrated
that exogenous LAs or LBs can competitively bind to surface FLP sites, thereby significantly
inhibiting their catalytic activity.65 As demonstrated in Figure 6a, the competitive introduction of
either LA inhibitors (pyrrole, boric acid) or LB inhibitors (pyridine, thiourea) into the reaction
system resulted in marked decreases in catalytic activity. These findings confirm the indispensable
role of bifunctional Cu⋯O FLP sites in the oxidative transformation of organosilanes, establishing
the crucial promoting effect of synergistic Lewis acid-base interactions on reaction conversion.

Our investigations conclusively identified the FLPs within the Cu cluster as the primary
4
active sites responsible for the observed catalytic transformation. This finding strongly suggests a
direct correlation between the catalytic activity of the FLPCluster system and the number of
accessible FLP sites. To rigorously verify this hypothesis, we loaded Cu and Cu clusters-each
22 28
confirmed by structural analysis to possess three well-defined FLP sites—onto carbon black
supports with an equivalent molar amount of FLP sites. Under identical reaction conditions,
catalytic test over a 6-hour period revealed significantly enhanced activity for both clusters,
reaching 1.5 and 1.5 times the benchmark activity of Cu , respectively (Figure 6b). Notably,
4
despite the differences in their overall size and structure, Cu and Cu clusters, which harbor the
22 28
identical number (three) of FLP sites, demonstrated remarkably comparable molar catalytic
activities. This key observation provides compelling evidence that the catalytic efficiency is
predominantly governed by the quantity of accessible FLP rather than the total cluster size or
structure. This conclusion is further reinforced by concentration-dependent experiments using the
Cu
4
catalyst: as the catalyst mass increased incrementally from 20 mg to 80 mg (maintaining a
constant loading ratio), the 6-hour conversion rates progressively rose from 15.6% to 32.6% and
68.4%, unambiguously demonstrating the dominant role of active site quantity in driving reaction
conversion (Figure S46). These collective results establish a critical and quantifiable relationship:
the catalytic efficiency on the surfaces of these copper clusters is intimately linked to, and primarily
determined by, the abundance of available FLP sites. This fundamental understanding provides a
robust foundation for the rational design and synthesis of next-generation, high-performance
copper cluster catalysts by strategically maximizing the density of these catalytically active FLP
centers.

To complement the experimental findings, we performed DFT calculations incorporating
Grimme’s dispersion correction to elucidate the reaction mechanism and determine accurate
adsorption energetics.66 The results reveal that water activation proceeds preferentially via
heterolytic cleavage: the hydroxyl group (OH) adsorbs on the copper center (LA site), while the
proton (H) coordinates to the oxygen atom (LB site) of the FLP (Supplementary Video 1). This
pathway is modestly endothermic (0.59 eV) with an activation barrier of 1.43 eV (Figure 6c,
IS→TS1→MS1). Although Cu and S atoms also form potential Lewis acid-base pairs, calculations
indicate they are catalytically inactive; water dissociation on these sites faces a prohibitively high
activation barrier of 2.36 eV (Figure S47), significantly higher than that of the Cu···O pathway.
Figure 6c illustrates the subsequent conversion of triethylsilane [(CH CH ) SiH] to triethylsilanol
3 2 3
mediated by the Cu⋯O FLP sites. Following exothermic silane adsorption (-0.46 eV, MS2), the
reaction proceeds through a transition state with a barrier of 0.92 eV. The subsequent formation of
the silanol product (MS4) involves dissociation of the intermediate, characterized by a barrier of
1.28 eV and a significant exothermic energy release of 1.23 eV. Desorption of the generated
(CH CH ) SiOH requires an energy input of 0.49 eV. Finally, the recombination of the proton on
3 2 3
the O site with the hydride on the Cu site generates H (FS) with a barrier of 0.75 eV and a reaction
2
energy of -1.30 eV. The catalytic cycle concludes with H desorption (0.50 eV), regenerating the
2
pristine Cu catalyst.

## Paper

## Abstract

FLPClusters, which are structurally precise metal clusters incorporating Frustrated
Lewis Pairs (FLPs), represent a promising class of FLP catalysts. Although FLPClusters have
emerged only recently, their precise and strategic synthesis remains underdeveloped. Herein, we
report the approach for the strategic synthesis of FLPClusters featuring well-defined, tailorable,
and accessible FLP active sites. Our approach utilizes bis(2-(diphenylphosphino)phenyl)ether
(DPEphos) as a rigid surface ligand. The two phosphine termini of DPEphos bridge adjacent metal
atoms, while the central ether oxygen atom (Lewis base) is geometrically constrained, enabling
the formation of stable FLPs with copper atoms (Lewis acid) on the cluster surface. By modulating
the structure of ancillary thiolate ligands, we successfully synthesized three FLPClusters.
These
FLPClusters demonstrate high catalytic activity in the hydrolytic oxidation of organosilanes to
silanols. Both theoretical and experimental studies confirm that the catalysis is FLP-driven.
Crucially, their catalytic performance scales with the number of FLP sites present.

---

## Introduction

Frustrated Lewis Pairs (FLPs) have attracted significant interest in chemical and materials
science.1-3 Comprising sterically or geometrically hindered Lewis acid (LA) and Lewis base (LB)
sites that cannot undergo classical adduct formation, FLPs exhibit a distinctive “push-pull” effect.4-
6 This enables efficient activation of diverse small molecules—including H , CO , SO , N O, NO,
2 2 2 2
and CO—leading to catalytic capabilities.7-10 A key advantage of FLPs lies in their exceptional
design flexibility: LB donors (e.g., N, O, S) and LA acceptors (e.g., B, Al, Ce, other metal centers)
offer broad tunability.11-14 Furthermore, the FLP concept extends beyond homogeneous catalysis,
proving compatible with heterogeneous systems such as zeolites, metal oxide surfaces, and
metal/covalent organic frameworks.15-17 These heterogeneous FLP catalysts demonstrate
remarkable efficiency and recyclability in small-molecule activation.18-21

The FLP concept has recently been introduced into the field of ligand-protected, atomically
precise noble metal clusters (designated as FLPClusters).22 Representing a promising class of
inorganic-organic hybrid materials, ligand-protected noble metal clusters exhibit broad
applications.23-32 Their atomically precise molecular structures, exceptional catalytic performance
across diverse chemical transformations, and structure-dependent catalytic properties establish
them as ideal model systems for investigating structure-catalysis relationships and reaction
mechanisms.33-37 Surface functionalization with tailored ligands has emerged as a strategy to create
FLP sites and enhance the catalytic performance of these metal clusters. For example,
incorporating 2-methoxybenzenethiolate ligands onto the [Cu S (RS) (PPh ) ]2+ cluster (Cu ,

RSH = 2-methoxybenzenethiol) facilitates the formation of FLPs between surface copper atoms
(acting as LAs) and the oxygen atoms of the ligands (acting as LBs).22 These precisely positioned

2

cycling stability, with no appreciable decay in activity observed over six consecutive cycles (18h
each) (Figure 5b).

To confirm the structural stability of the catalysts, a suite of characterization techniques was
employed. The structural evolution of the clusters under operating conditions was probed by X-
ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure
(EXAFS) measurements at the Cu K-edge. The spectral profiles of Cu remained virtually identical
4
before and after loading onto carbon black, confirming that immobilization did not alter the
cluster’s nuclearity or geometry (Figure S37a). Crucially, the XANES and EXAFS features of the
catalyst were preserved after the reaction (Figure S37b, c). Quantitative EXAFS fitting (Figure
S38 and Table S5) revealed no significant deviations in the coordination numbers or bond lengths
of the Cu–Cu, Cu–S and Cu–P shells, proving that the cluster framework remains intact without
aggregation or fragmentation. This conclusion is corroborated by transmission electron
microscopy (TEM), which showed no formation of metal nanoparticles, and XPS and FTIR
spectroscopy, which verified the preservation of the Cu oxidation state and ligand coordination
environment (Figures S39–S42).

Comparative analysis identifies the engineered surface FLP sites as the sole origin of the
enhanced catalytic activity. The DPEphos ligand plays a dual role: it passivates the cluster to
maintain structural integrity while its central oxygen atom acts as a geometrically constrained
Lewis base, cooperating with surface copper atoms to form active FLP sites. To rigorously verify
this mechanism, we designed a series of control experiments (Figure 5c). Neither the carbon black
support nor the free DPEphos ligand exhibited significant activity (conversions < 5%). Similarly,
physical mixtures of copper salts and DPEphos showed negligible activity (5.8%). These results
collectively rule out the carbon support, free ligands, or unstructured copper species as active
contributors. Compelling evidence is provided by structurally well-defined Cu derivatives
4
stabilized by non-FLP ligands—specifically Cu (PPh Py) Cl and Cu (dpph) (PhC≡C) —which
4 2 4 2 4 2 4
exhibited only moderate activity (7.5% and 8.4% conversion, respectively) due to the absence of
accessible FLP motifs (Figures 5c and S43).58,59 Similarly, conventional copper nanoclusters
passivated by non-functional ligands (Cu (9.5%), Cu (6.2%), Cu (6.8%), Cu (6.0%), Cu
25 26 8 50 12
(6.4%), and Cu (7.3%)) showed negligible activity (Figures 5c, S44 and S45).60-64 These findings
66
collectively demonstrate that the catalytic performance is not an intrinsic property of the copper
cluster core, but originates exclusively from the geometrically well-defined FLP sites established
by the precise coordination of DPEphos to the surface copper centers. Notably, the Cu /XC-72
4
catalyst also exhibits a broad substrate scope under optimized conditions, effectively oxidizing
diverse silane substrates with equally high efficiency (Figure 5d). Impressively, the catalyst
achieves complete oxidation of both sterically hindered alkylsilanes and electronically distinct
arylsilanes without observable differences in rate attributable to steric effects.

Reaction mechanism of silane hydrolysis catalyzed by FLPClusters. To fully elucidate
the fundamental characteristics of surface FLPs and their catalytic mechanism, we adopted an
integrated approach combining experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT)
calculations. Initially, molecular probe-based active site blocking experiments were conducted to
investigate the active site dependence of the catalytic reaction. Previous studies have demonstrated
that exogenous LAs or LBs can competitively bind to surface FLP sites, thereby significantly
inhibiting their catalytic activity.65 As demonstrated in Figure 6a, the competitive introduction of
either LA inhibitors (pyrrole, boric acid) or LB inhibitors (pyridine, thiourea) into the reaction
system resulted in marked decreases in catalytic activity. These findings confirm the indispensable
role of bifunctional Cu⋯O FLP sites in the oxidative transformation of organosilanes, establishing
the crucial promoting effect of synergistic Lewis acid-base interactions on reaction conversion.

Our investigations conclusively identified the FLPs within the Cu cluster as the primary
4
active sites responsible for the observed catalytic transformation. This finding strongly suggests a
direct correlation between the catalytic activity of the FLPCluster system and the number of
accessible FLP sites. To rigorously verify this hypothesis, we loaded Cu and Cu clusters-each
22 28
confirmed by structural analysis to possess three well-defined FLP sites—onto carbon black
supports with an equivalent molar amount of FLP sites. Under identical reaction conditions,
catalytic test over a 6-hour period revealed significantly enhanced activity for both clusters,
reaching 1.5 and 1.5 times the benchmark activity of Cu , respectively (Figure 6b). Notably,
4
despite the differences in their overall size and structure, Cu and Cu clusters, which harbor the
22 28
identical number (three) of FLP sites, demonstrated remarkably comparable molar catalytic
activities. This key observation provides compelling evidence that the catalytic efficiency is
predominantly governed by the quantity of accessible FLP rather than the total cluster size or
structure. This conclusion is further reinforced by concentration-dependent experiments using the
Cu
4
catalyst: as the catalyst mass increased incrementally from 20 mg to 80 mg (maintaining a
constant loading ratio), the 6-hour conversion rates progressively rose from 15.6% to 32.6% and
68.4%, unambiguously demonstrating the dominant role of active site quantity in driving reaction
conversion (Figure S46). These collective results establish a critical and quantifiable relationship:
the catalytic efficiency on the surfaces of these copper clusters is intimately linked to, and primarily
determined by, the abundance of available FLP sites. This fundamental understanding provides a
robust foundation for the rational design and synthesis of next-generation, high-performance
copper cluster catalysts by strategically maximizing the density of these catalytically active FLP
centers.

To complement the experimental findings, we performed DFT calculations incorporating
Grimme’s dispersion correction to elucidate the reaction mechanism and determine accurate
